item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — “artificial intelligence model” is undefined.** Companies could characterize a product as an algorithm, agent, service, ensemble, or other system rather than a “model,” creating threshold litigation.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — “trained” and “training run” are undefined.** The bill does not say whether pretraining, post-training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, distillation, continual learning, or automated architecture search counts as training.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — the single-run limitation invites compute splitting.** A developer could divide training among multiple nominal runs, models, entities, or stages, each below \(10^{26}\) operations, and subsequently combine the results.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — the compute threshold is not aggregation-resistant.** The text does not aggregate compute used for failed runs, checkpoint restarts, precursor models, synthetic-data generation, or related components of one development project.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — operation counting is unspecified and manipulable.** There is no prescribed methodology for counting operations, handling sparsity or mixture-of-experts models, or distinguishing integer and floating-point operations of different precisions.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — exactly \(10^{26}\) operations is excluded.** Because the definition says “greater than,” a run using exactly the threshold amount is not covered.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — the fixed statutory threshold will become obsolete.** Hardware, algorithms, and training methods may produce dangerous capabilities below \(10^{26}\) operations, but no agency can lower or otherwise update the threshold.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — the threshold is difficult to prove.** The bill imposes no compute-metering, log-retention, chip-reporting, or audit requirements on developers, leaving the government dependent on company records to establish coverage.

9. **Section 2(1)(B) — “the Secretary” is never identified.** It could mean the Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of State mentioned later, or another official, potentially invalidating or delaying capability determinations.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — the capability standard is highly indeterminate.** “Substantially exceeding,” “human performance,” “most,” and “cognitive tasks” lack benchmarks, reference populations, task weights, and testing conditions, making determinations inconsistent and vulnerable to vagueness challenges.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — coverage depends on an affirmative agency determination.** A highly capable system remains outside subparagraph (B) until the Secretary acts, allowing development and deployment during testing, investigation, and litigation.

12. **Section 2(1)(B) — there is no determination process.** The bill provides no authority to demand access or evaluations, issue emergency or preliminary determinations, prescribe tests, revisit systems after capability improvements, or require developers to disclose evidence of capability.

13. **Section 2(1)(B) — the legal effect and timing of determinations are unclear.** The bill does not address notice, publication, appeals, retroactivity, or whether copies, modified versions, successors, and systems incorporating the designated system are also covered.

14. **Section 2(1)(B) — the delegation lacks meaningful standards.** Giving an unidentified Secretary discretion to decide which systems are prohibited, without procedures or limiting principles beyond vague capability language, invites nondelegation, major-questions, and due-process challenges.

15. **Section 2(2) — “U.S. person” omits many relevant people and entities.** It excludes permanent residents, U.S. nationals who are not citizens, partnerships, unincorporated associations, trusts, federally or territorially organized entities, and foreign subsidiaries controlled by U.S. companies.

16. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a) — “person” is separately undefined.** Section 3 applies domestically to “any person,” but the bill does not incorporate the usual statutory definition covering individuals, corporations, partnerships, associations, and government entities.

17. **Section 2(3) — “data center” and “advanced AI chip” are undefined.** Operators could dispute whether particular campuses, buildings, leased suites, accelerators, custom chips, or older chips constitute a covered facility.

18. **Section 2(3) — the facility threshold is easy to evade.** A project can distribute 50,000 or fewer chips among adjacent buildings, affiliated operators, or multiple cloud regions because the bill contains no aggregation or anti-circumvention rule.

19. **Section 2(3) — exactly 50,000 chips is excluded.** “More than 50,000” leaves facilities containing precisely 50,000 chips outside the registry.

20. **Section 2(3) — chip counting lacks a time and control rule.** The provision does not say whether disconnected, warehoused, leased, temporarily installed, remotely pooled, or jointly controlled chips count, or when the threshold is measured.

21. **Section 3(a) — the prohibited conduct is undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” have no statutory meanings, leaving uncertainty over research, fine-tuning, testing, integration, API service, internal use, and publication of model weights.

22. **Section 3(a) — important enabling conduct is not expressly prohibited.** The text does not clearly bar possessing, acquiring, importing, exporting, selling, licensing, transferring, financing, hosting, maintaining, operating, or providing chips, data, weights, or technical assistance for a covered system.

23. **Section 3(a) — distributed and intermediary responsibility is unclear.** Cloud providers, chip lessors, data-center operators, contractors, investors, and open-source distributors may argue that they did not themselves train, develop, or deploy the system.

24. **Section 3(a) — there are no attempt, conspiracy, aiding-and-abetting, or anti-evasion provisions.** The government may have difficulty intervening before training is completed or reaching coordinated schemes structured through nominally independent actors.

25. **Section 3(a) — extraterritorial application is incomplete.** It covers U.S. citizens and state-organized corporations abroad, but not foreign subsidiaries controlled by them, U.S. residents who are not citizens, or foreign projects directed, funded, or supplied from the United States.

26. **Section 3(a) — prohibited-system handling is unaddressed.** The bill does not require shutdown, secure custody, destruction of weights and checkpoints, recall of distributed copies, or prevention of continued inference after a violation.

27. **Section 3(b) — the grandfather clause swallows the prohibition.** If any training “began” before enactment, the entire covered system is exempt from all of subsection (a), apparently including later development and deployment.

28. **Section 3(b) — “training began” is undefined and easily manufactured.** A company could claim that an early experiment, token preliminary run, old checkpoint, or trivial training step began the training of a much later system.

29. **Section 3(b) — derivatives and successors are unresolved.** The text does not say whether retrained versions, fine-tunes, merged models, copies, new checkpoints, or systems built around a grandfathered model inherit the exemption.

30. **Section 3(b) — no grandfathered-system controls exist.** Even genuinely existing systems are subject to no registration, capability limits, security requirements, transfer restrictions, or prohibition on scaling them further.

31. **Section 3(c) — the safety-evaluation exemption is unlimited and subjective.** Any actor can claim a prohibited activity was conducted “for the purpose” of safety evaluation; there is no approval requirement, objective necessity test, compute limit, duration limit, or rule for mixed motives.

32. **Section 3(c) — exempt work can itself create or release a dangerous system.** The provision does not restrict deployment, external access, retention or transfer of weights, cybersecurity, personnel, facilities, or disposition of the system after an evaluation.

33. **Section 4(a) — “operator” is undefined.** Owners, tenants, cloud providers, colocation companies, and customers may each deny being the party obligated to register.

34. **Section 4(a) — registration mechanics are absent.** There is no registration deadline, required information, update obligation, deregistration rule, or authority for Commerce to prescribe forms and procedures.

35. **Section 4 — registry violations carry no stated penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3, so failure to register, report, or report truthfully is not expressly subject to the Act’s civil or criminal penalties.

36. **Section 4 — the registry covers facilities, not dangerous compute projects.** Below-threshold facilities, distributed clusters, overseas facilities used by U.S. persons, chip owners, cloud customers, and compute brokers have no registration or reporting duty.

37. **Section 4(b) — workload reports are too vague.** “Describing the computing workloads” specifies no data fields, granularity, compute-accounting method, customer identification, model information, reporting deadline, or record-retention period.

38. **Section 4(b) — “certified by the operator” supplies little assurance.** The bill does not identify a responsible certifying officer, specify the certification’s content or knowledge standard, or expressly make false certifications punishable under the Act.

39. **Sections 3–5 — no regulator is assigned to administer the prohibition.** The bill gives no agency clear responsibility or authority to issue rules, investigate suspected systems, compel information, inspect facilities, or coordinate enforcement.

40. **Sections 3–5 — essential enforcement remedies are missing.** There is no express authority for injunctions, emergency stop-work orders, chip or model seizure, forfeiture, license revocation, debarment, or compelled deletion, so monetary penalties may not stop an imminent training run.

41. **Sections 3–5 — no monitoring or verification regime exists.** The bill does not require chip manufacturers, cloud providers, developers, or utilities to report large clusters or training runs, and provides no tamper-resistant metering or independent audits.

42. **Sections 3–5 — no rulemaking, subpoena, inspection, or appropriations authority is provided.** Commerce may lack the tools and resources needed to operationalize the definitions, registry, and enforcement program.

43. **Section 5(a) — the civil penalty may be economically inadequate.** “Not more than” $1 million per day permits nominal penalties, and even the maximum may be trivial relative to the value of a frontier project; there is no per-chip, per-system, revenue-based, or gain-based penalty.

44. **Section 5(a) — “each day” does not fit all violations.** A completed training run, one-time weight transfer, or instantaneous deployment may produce only a single day of penalties even though the resulting system remains available indefinitely.

45. **Section 5(a) — no civil enforcement procedure is specified.** The text does not identify who assesses or sues for penalties, what process applies, where actions may be brought, or what limitation period governs.

46. **Section 5(b) — “willfully” may impose an unnecessarily difficult burden.** Defendants may argue that the government must prove knowledge that the conduct was unlawful, especially given the bill’s vague definitions and uncertain agency determinations.

47. **Section 5(b) — responsibility within organizations is unclear.** The bill does not specify liability for executives, directors, controlling persons, or responsible corporate officers who authorize or recklessly disregard a violation.

48. **Sections 5 and 8 — the penalty date conflicts with the effective date.** Section 5 purports to cover violations on or after enactment, while section 8 says the Act takes effect 180 days later, creating uncertainty about whether any conduct during that period is prohibited or punishable.

49. **Section 6 — the international-negotiation duty is weak and unenforceable.** “Shall seek to negotiate” requires neither an agreement nor meaningful progress, and “equivalent” prohibitions are undefined.

50. **Section 6 — the deadline is grammatically ambiguous.** “Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” could require only that negotiations be initiated by then, not pursued continuously or completed, and there is no reporting requirement if talks fail.

51. **Section 7(a) — the termination standard is vague.** “Can be developed safely” gives no required degree of safety, evidence, time horizon, threat model, or burden of proof.

52. **Section 7(a) — the National Academies process is unspecified.** No one is directed to request or fund the report, no deadline or required contents are provided, and the text does not say whether Congress may act without a favorable report.

53. **Section 7(a) — the joint-resolution mechanism lacks procedures.** The bill does not identify the resolution’s required text or provide introduction, committee, debate, amendment, or expedited-consideration rules; “acting on a report” is also undefined.

54. **Section 7 — subsections (a) and (b) undermine each other.** Section 7(a) suggests the prohibition lasts until an affirmative congressional safety finding, but subsection (b) automatically ends the entire Act after 10 years even if no such finding occurs.

55. **Section 7(b) — the sunset terminates more than the prohibition.** It eliminates the registry, reporting duties, penalties, and international-agreement provision as well as section 3, leaving no continuing oversight of systems or facilities after year ten.

56. **Section 7(b) — there is no savings clause.** Sunset could jeopardize pending investigations, accrued penalties, prosecutions, reporting records, and continuing remedial orders for pre-sunset violations.

57. **Section 8 — the 180-day delay permits accelerated development.** Companies can use the grace period to rearrange facilities, move work offshore, distribute compute, and begin projects that may later invoke ambiguities in the grandfather clause, without interim reporting or preservation duties.
